subtopic: MR. MATHER-REPLY OF POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING INCREASED POSTAL RATES
MR. MATHER-REPLY OF POSTMASTER GENERAL RESPECTING INCREASED POSTAL RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday on orders of the day I sought to ask the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) whether in the event that the ordinary Canadian first class letter rate is increased, as the government proposes, from 5 cents to 6 cents, he would seek to have the international postal rate governing Canadian letters increased likewise; otherwise I said it would cost more to mail a letter from Ottawa to, say, Toronto than from Ottawa to Los Angeles, the present international rate being 5 cents.
My question was ruled out of order. However, at the conclusion of orders of the day the minister rose in his place and stated, as I heard him, that the basis of my question was false. I understand the minister's views, having discussed this matter with him yesterday at the conclusion of orders of the day. However, my point of privilege is that my question, or any part of it, was not false or wrong.
The present Canadian letter rate is 5 cents and it may be increased to 6 cents. Unless the international rate is likewise increased it will indeed cost more to mail a letter from Ottawa to any point in Canada than from Ottawa to the United States. Under the circumstances the words "false" or "wrong" are not acceptable.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Registrar General) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs; to provide for the appointment of a minister and a deputy minister and for their duties and powers; to provide that the governor in council may establish a consumer advisory council and other bodies to assist the minister and for the remuneration and expenses of the members thereof; and to provide for certain other matters related or incidental thereto.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Batten in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend
to speak at any great length at the resolution
3068	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs stage of this measure. The bill itself is not yet before the house. I know that under the rules and practices of this house a resolution is required whenever there is a fiscal or monetary feature attached to a bill involving a charge upon the consolidated revenue fund. I might say, however, that the fiscal features of this particular bill are rather subordinate to its main purposes, one of which is to reorganize the Department of the Registrar General and convert it into a department of corporate and consumer affairs.
I intend, Mr. Chairman, if the committee will allow me, to make a full presentation on second reading if the house adopts this resolution today. The resolution stage has now been reduced to one day under the rules of this house. I am most anxious to hear what hon. members have to say at this stage of the proceedings. At one time the resolution was required for traditional and historical reasons, when the Commons went to the monarch and asked for permission to introduce a bill involving money, but without in any way suggesting that the debate should be restricted, I am led to wonder if this practice has not become rather an appendix of history.
In any event I intend to get down to the issues at some length on second reading, so this morning I will confine myself to saying that the principal aim of the legislation proposed in this resolution is to achieve a further rationalization of the organization of government at the federal level. I believe, sir, that a significant step was taken earlier, when the Department of the Registrar General was established in 1966, at which time we brought together for the first time a number of functions relating to corporations, combines, patents, trade marks and bankruptcies, in order to ensure the better co-ordination of policy in these fields.

Mr. Chairman, the aim of this legislation is to promote co-ordination in the field of consumer affairs. In the past, the activities of the federal government with regard to the protection or information of consumers were divided between several departments, that is to say there never was any co-ordinated program or, if I may be allowed to use that term, any appeal court for the consumers who wanted help or information from the federal government 
DEBATES	October 13, 1967
[DOT] (11:40 a.m.)

I think the need has now become evident, Mr. Chairman. The consumers association of Canada appealed to the government as early as 1960 and on numerous later occasions to create a department which would be responsible for the interests of consumers. Members of the committee will recall that the matter was also studied by the special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on consumer credit and the cost of living during the fall and winter of 1966-67. In its interim report in December, 1966 the committee, ably chaired by Senator Croll and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, firmly endorsed the concept of a department to be responsible for consumer affairs.
During the period of the joint committee's hearings the federal government's responsibility in the field of consumer affairs was being investigated by the Economic Council of Canada. The economic council's examination arose, as members know, from the formal request by the government in July, 1966 that the council study and advise regarding the interests of the consumer, particularly as they relate to the functions of the Department of the Registrar General. There were other issues as well which were raised in this reference, those relating to combines, mergers and restrictive trade practices and those relating to patents, trade marks and copyrights.
Last summer, in July 1967, the economic council issued an interim report in which it concluded, among other things, that the primary responsibility for consumer affairs should be centred in the Department of the Registrar General. The view of the economic council, with which I completely concur, is that the federal government's consumer program could be administered more efficiently through improved co-ordination.
The opinion that consumers need a more adequate voice in government has received parliamentary support. It has received support from independent agencies as well as a wide measure of support, I believe, from the Canadian public. It is the purpose of this proposed legislation to ensure that the voices of the consumer, whether those voices be organized or unorganized, will be listened to. To our mind, Mr. Chairman, the most effective way of achieving this is to streamline and rationalize both the channels of communication and federal activities in the whole field of consumer affairs.
October 13, 1967

The house will note, as well, that the resolution provides for the establishment of a consumer advisory council as recommended by the Economic Council of Canada in its interim report of last July. I feel that such an advisory council will be greatly helpful, not only to the minister but also to the department, in our efforts to help the Canadian consumer.
I shall have more to say about that during the debate on second reading of the bill. I shall describe what we now plan for the overall program.

The proposal to include both consumer affairs and corporate affairs within one department calls for an explanatory comment once again. In my defence of the estimates before the house rose for the summer adjournment I recall that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway had a good deal to say about this question. I will not repeat what I said in anticipation of her argument at that time, sir, but I would say that corporate affairs in this context, in the context of the reorganization envisaged by this bill, refer to certain specialized functions of the federal government relating to corporations and corporate securities, to combines, mergers, monopolies, restraint of trade, bankruptcy, insolvency, patents, copyrights and trade marks.
One of the main purposes of the Corporations Act is to help protect the investing public. In the same sense the purpose of the Combines Investigation Act is to ensure that businessmen large and small and the general public are not damaged by the improper use of market power. Creditors in turn benefit from regulations governing bankruptcy and insolvency, and thus improvements have to be made there in both the administration and, of course, the law itself.

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
I said that in order to represent the demand side of the market place and to give the consumer and investor a direct voice in governmental affairs, any department charged with that responsibility would have to have some authority over certain aspects of the supply side of the market place. Those aspects of the supply side of the market place are covered within the corporate affairs functions of this department.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that at a time when parliament and the public are quite properly concerned about the level of government expenditures it is sensible and economical to convert the Department of the Registrar General into a department of corporate and consumer affairs rather than to duplicate in an entirely new department the administrative and other central services that any department must have. I think in this way we can bring to bear on the problems of the consumer some of the experience and expertise of the older branches of government, particularly the combines branch.
We will be recruiting a small number of carefully selected officials in the field of consumer affairs, but much of our work will take the form of ensuring the co-ordination of existing governmental activity; we have no intention of building up a vast new bureaucracy.

I trust the house will agree that the report of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, and the interim report of the Economic Council of Canada and other public bodies, pointed out the necessity of creating a department to represent and promote the interest of the consumers. I also trust this committee will give its whole-hearted support to the resolution.

speechtext:
The hon. member says "Utter nonsense", but the words in the resolution make it clear that the government wants to establish a consumer advisory council. We already have an Economic Council of Canada which has made certain recommendations in connection with consumer affairs, recommendations which incidentally are not being followed by the government. The minister passed very lightly over the real reasons for establishing the department. He did not deal with the specific recommendations of the economic council. He did not explain to this committee why the advice of the economic council was not being followed. The economic council made specific recommendations knowing full well what were the recommendations made by the special committee which the minister praised. That committee may have recommended that a new department be set up. However, in the knowledge that the committee had made such a recommendation the economic council took pains to disagree.
There is certainly a need for co-ordination. The economic council points this out on pages 19 and 20 of its interim report. I would specifically draw the attention of the minister to what appears at the top of page 20, where the economic council has this to say:
The implementation of these recomendations does not require a vast expansion in government activity and in the size of the bureaucracy. Any such tendencies should be strongly resisted as being neither necessary nor wise.

DEBATES	October 13, 1967
The reference in the first line is to the recommendations of the economic council. In spite of this the decision of the government has been to press right ahead with the proliferation of the bureaucracy, which is about to progress in true Parkinsonian fashion, to use another of the economic council's phrases. A little further on the council has this to say:
In view of the wide scope of consumer interests and the many departments which are engaged in activities affecting consumers, there is no possibility of concentrating all these activities in a single department, nor would it be desirable to try to do so.
How well I remember those now occupying the treasury benches, particularly the Minister of Finance, castigating the previous government for its failure to follow advice. Here they are flying in the teeth of advice given to them by eminent experts in the fields of labour, economics and industry. What the economic council does recommend-and it is put into words a little later on page 20-is this:
A great improvement in present methods of co-ordination is necesary, and for this purpose we recommend the establishment of an interdepartmental committee on consumer affairs under the chairmanship of the deputy registrar general. The committee should include the deputy ministers of trade and commerce, national health and welfare, industry, agriculture, fisheries, insurance, finance and justice and such other departments as have a continuing interest in consumer matters.
Note that the council does not recommend the setting up of a new department. The minister may very well reply to this argument by saying it is not the intention of the government to appoint a separate minister but that the department will be administered by himself. This is no guarantee that a separate minister will not be appointed at some time in the future. The government might change its mind. The hon. gentleman cannot in honesty rise and give an assurance that a minister will not be appointed at some time in the future to handle the affairs of this department. He cannot do so, if only for the reason that if the bill passes, subsequent governments would not be bound by such an assurance.
There is, however, to be a deputy minister, according to the resolution and it does, in fact, represent a proliferation of the bureaucracy. The council went on to recommend- This committee should have a permanent secretariat within the department of the Registrar General which would asist in the work of the committee and in keeping the minister informed of federal government activities in the field of consumer affairs.
October 13, 1967

The minister took pains to say it is not the intention of the government to propagate bureaucracy, if I may paraphrase his words but this in effect is what he and his colleagues are doing. The government can almost be described as promiscuous in this area of propagating new departments. If they need advice they get it. They receive specific recommendations, but they do not follow those recommendations. One would almost be constrained to prescribe the pill for them to end this profligate conduct of the government.
On page 22 the economic council goes on to say it has-
-carefully considered the advantages and disadvantages of transferring responsibilities for other existing federal government functions to the Registrar General and recommends that at the present time only a few such transfers be made. This decision should, however, be subject to review after a period of experience in the operation of the new Department of the Registrar General.
Not, hon. members will note, of a department of consumers affairs.
At that time, in the light of what has been achieved in the way of improved performance-
Having regard to the past performance of this government I doubt whether the optimism of the council here can be accepted
-and co-ordination of consumer functions by the federal government, the question can be considered whether further transfers of such functions to the Registrar General should be made.
[DOT] (12 noon)
The next phrase is very important. The council says:
If the present recommendations of the Economic Council are accepted, they should not require any significant net growth in the federal public service. Our emphasis is on the improved organization, rearrangement and co-ordination of activities, and not on the proliferation of staff engaged in these functions.
How in the world can the government justify itself in flying in the teeth of that kind of recommendation?
In the fourth annual report of the council they were quite concerned over government expenditures. On page 260 of that report they expressed their concern in these words:
It is also a striking fact that, in spite of the very large increases in defence expenditures which took place in the United States in 1965 and 1966 as a result of the increased involvement in Viet Nam, government spending rose more rapidly in Canada than in the United States in these two years. Over the period 1963-66, total government expenditures at all levels of government rose by about 25 per cent in the United States and about 35 per cent in Canada. Total non-defence government expenditures now represent nearly 30 per
Corporate and Consumer Affairs cent of gross national product in Canada, but only about 20 per cent in the United States-a difference reflecting, among other things, relatively higher expenditures in Canada for social welfare, transportation, interest on the public debt and subsidies.
On page 261 of the report these words appear:
These developments have led to a growing uneasiness in Canada about the current pace of the over-all advance in government spending. The council shares this uneasiness-
And they refer to the Parkinsonian buildup of the bureaucracy. I commend this report and these recommendations to the minister and to the government. Why are they not being followed? It seems to me that the recommendation of the council that a very careful approach be made to the problem of organization and co-ordination is an extremely reasonable one, but the government leaps in with both feet and is again incurring large expenditures in the creation of a separate department.
The minister might say, "Well, your fears are unfounded." He might even give us an estimate of the amount that is going to be spent, the anticipated cost of the functioning of the new department. However, we had that experience at the time of the creation of the Department of Industry when we in this house were led to believe that it was only going to cost $35 million to operate that new department. Now the cost is well over $100 million and is still rising. This is what is going to happen here.
The economic council put it this way on page 27 of their interim report:
In summary, the proposed functions of the emerging Department of the Registrar General in the field of consumer affairs are co-ordination, research and information activities, representation of the consumer interest, and the administration of a limited number of laws affecting both trade and financial matters. It is not anticipated nor intended that a substantial increase in the size of government staff should be necessary to perform these functions satisfactorily.
The council concludes on page 29 of its report:
The above recommendations constitute a number of practical steps towards better organized and more effective consumer policies in Canada. Among other things, they give to the Department of the Registrar General, in the field of consumer affairs, a central co-ordinating role within the federal government and a coherent group of operating responsibilities. This should help to provide a sound administrative base for the future pursuit of consumer policies.
Flying in the teeth of those recommendations the government sets up a new department. When the minister closes this debate he
October 13, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs may make, as I am sure he will, the most honest and sincere attempts to reconcile our fears that this new department is going to result in what the council calls a Parkinsonian growth of the bureaucracy. But he cannot allay mine. I would really like to be convinced.
There are 24 ministers now and this new department will mean 25. Another for housing and urban development will increase the number to 26. The race is on, and all the time the consumer price index is going up. This government is one of high costs.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as we debate this resolution the cost of living is rising steadily. The hon. member who has just preceded me has drawn attention to the figures in the index. I have here the issue of the Financial Post for October 7 in which it is pointed out that there has been an accelerating decline in the value of our dollar and what it will buy in Canada now. The article states that the Canadian dollar of 1925 is barely worth 50 cents today and that inflation is clearly evident on the housing front where the price of new houses financed under N.H.A. has risen by almost one third during the past four years. It mentions that after a slower rise last fall and winter consumer prices are again moving up quickly and that the rate of advance now is almost as rapid as it was in the inflationary months of 1965-66. The article goes on to say:
Higher food prices were behind most of the big rise of consumer prices in 1965-66 and, although edging up again, are not as big a push force as other components of living costs.
The heaviest pressure now on consumer prices comes from services. Most stable prices for a decade have been those of manufactured goods. But with narrowing profit margins, producers are currently pushing up the prices of a widening range of items.
The Financial Post sums up by saying:
Consumer prices are rising quickly once again and this time it's an across-the-board advance.
What does this mean? It means that the consumers of Canada are finding themselves naked and defenceless before the winds of heaven. They have appealed to this government for help time and time again over the past few years, and they have appealed with increased urgency as the cost of living has been rising. As the minister pointed out, since 1960 the consumer association of Canada has been asking for a department of consumer affairs. In 1964 my colleague, the hon. member for Danforth, urged in the house the need for a department of consumer affairs. In 1965 it was my colleague from Bumaby-Richmond who again put forth the demand of consumers for a department to manage their affairs. Last year I was the spokesman in respect of this demand. Outside parliament many other voices have been raised.
The consumers of Canada have consistently and urgently appealed to this government for help but again the winds of heaven have left them naked and defenceless. What are they being given? They are being given more wind, and some of the wind has taken the form of pretty severe and harsh blasts. I refer to the rise from 7J per cent to 8i per cent in
3074	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs the N.H.A. mortgage rate. I refer to the complete ignoring of the plight of the consumers in the budget and in the government's explanation of that budget. I refer to the stubborn delay and resistance in respect of dealing with matters such as veterans' pensions, an increase in old age pensions and every other attempt on the part of the consumers to protect themselves by getting their incomes raised to meet the onslaught of rising prices and the cost of living.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The consumer has never been so helpless as far as the market place is concerned as he is today. The consumer has lost control of the market place. Those of us who were members of the consumer committee understood things very plainly. We found that no longer is there any real competition in the market. At the present time three or four major corporations dominate every field in the market place. They control the situation completely. They plan everything down to the finest detail and completely control the consumer. In the tobacco field there are four companies. In the meat packing business there are three companies. Three companies dominate the soap business and five companies dominate the farm implement business, although not each of them has the same power.
Let me refer to an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail on December 20, 1966 in relation to chain store merchandising. The heading is "New Figures Show Weston's World's No. 2 Merchandiser." It begins by stating:
The Garfield Weston world wide food empire, which sprouted from a bakery shop in West Toronto, now ranks second in profit among all merchandising organizations and third in sales.

Mr. Chairman, the matter of consumer credit is nothing new. In fact, it was raised in the house several years ago and it has been discussed year after year. Today, a resolution is placed before us, which reads as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs; to provide for the appointment of a minister and a deputy minister and for their duties and powers; to provide that the governor in council may establish a consumer advisory council and other bodies to assist the minister and for the remuneration and expenses of the members thereof; and to provide for certain other matters related or incidental thereto.
That resolution is introduced by the Registrar General (Mr. Turner). It is not a bill, it is not a piece of legislation, it is simply a resolution asking, as it were, for permission to introduce a piece of legislation.
Mr. Chairman, for the last few years, we have witnessed the creation of various bodies as, for instance, the Economic Council of Canada, study commissions and consumers organizations, to consider consumer credit, but we have never come to a conclusion or found a solution to the problem of consumer credit.
Still, we who support the creditiste doctrine have repeatedly proposed a solution that could be put to the test so that we might see its results. We know the results of present procedures; they are disastrous and prove clearly that the Canadian consumer now faces debts for years to come.
The average worker mortgages his salary for two, three, four, or five years, or even for 10, 15 or 25 years when he buys a small property.
Mr. Chairman, we all know that producers stand on one side, and consumers on the other. There are middlemen between the two
3078	COMMONS
Corporate and Consumer Affairs who provide services, or enable the goods to reach the consumers. Everyone understands that. Some blame the middle man and say, like the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis), that the big fellow makes too much profit while the little fellow pays too much for the goods he buys, so that the rich get richer and the poor get poorer.
Would direct intervention by the government in placing a ceiling on prises and wages solve this problem? Prices and wages were controlled in this way during the war, and the immediate result was the birth of the black market, an inevitable phenomenon on any market or in any country in the world. The black market arises from coercion or control exercized by the government on production, wages and consumption.
Mr. Chairman, there is a difference between a person who can pay cash and one who must ask for credit in just about every sphere of economic activity. If a Canadian consumer buys goods worth $1,000, whether it be furniture, or a car, or anything else, he will get a 20 per cent discount if he pays cash.
: Everyone more or less agrees with this. However, if the same consumer must buy on credit or finance his purchases, the same goods worth $1,000 will cost him at least $1,180, because of the interest on his loan or instalment plan. This means a difference of $380 for $1,000 worth of goods.
This means a 38 per cent difference between paying cash and buying on credit. Some may say that people have to buy on credit. Yes, they have to, because they do not have the purchasing power necessary to pay cash. That is the reason. No one would buy on credit if everyone had the money to pay cash.
That is where the creditistes suggest a solution. There is only one way to enable Canadian consumers to buy products made in Canada or existing products, and that is by giving them more purchasing power without at the same time raising the price of goods.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Today, there are several strikes going on. They are called for better working conditions, of course, but mostly for higher wages; however, as soon as a salary raise is granted, it must be added to production costs and, as a result, prices go up. Once more, salaries lag behind prices and the whole process starts over again. It is a vicious circle from which we can never hope to extricate ourselves.
Mr. Chairman, a new department of consumer affairs may be created, an da consumer
[Mr. Caouette.l

advisory council, but I think we have no need for all that, because we already know what the consumer wants. In fact, we could appoint ten ministers of consumer affairs but we would get the same results if we retained the same system.
No matter how many ministers or advisers are appointed, how many commissions, committees or advisory boards are created. I still believe that so long as we keep the present financial system, no solution will be found for the problems facing us and we will keep on witnessing this spiralling race between prices and wages and wages and prices.
Even if the ministers and all the civil servants of this new department go ahead with the establishment of wage and price controls, the black market will remain and will push the cost of living even higher.
Mr. Chairman, for a long time now we have been explaining the situation in parliament and the search is still going on; dilly-dallying, looking for solutions within a system lacking the possibility of settling the problem. The government is the first to suffer from this system because it is not in a position to give one cent to the people or to the Canadian consumer without having to pay interest to the Canadian banking system. The government is not in a position to undertake any construction whatever without having to kneel before the financiers to beg permission to develop our country. Yet, there is talk of helping the consumers to improve their living condition and preventing evil capitalists from making profits.
Mr. Chairman, we have a solution to offer in order to restore order between production and consumption, between prices and the people's incomes: firstly, a compensated discount on retail prices allowed by the government, but charged to the Bank of Canada rather than being included in taxes. Such discount would not be included in the price of goods and would compensate the retail price. Thus, the consumer would get a rebate and his purchasing power would be increased without injuring anyone. Retailers, dealers and manufacturers would still be making profits, because it is not manufacturers' or dealers' profits that prevent consumers from sharing in the Canadian production, it is the monetary system.
If profit is an incentive for individual effort, for private enterprise, for the economic development of our country, one should consider it rather favourably, instead of forever attacking it.
October 13, 1967

We sincerely believe, Mr. Chairman, that the compensated discount paid by the Bank of Canada through a national credit board, would considerably help Canadian consumers to maintain a balance between purchasing power and production.
Secondly, so that all Canadian consumers, from the social, economic and political standpoints, obtain and receive the assurance of a guaranteed vital minimum, we would suggest the distribution of a national dividend based on national production and distributed through the credit board; the latter would request the Bank of Canada to issue the required cheques in order to increase the consumers' purchasing power, but this dividend would not be added to the cost of goods. Thus, we would increase the consumers' purchasing power without raising prices. This is the opposite of what is happening today.
But, Mr. Chairman, when we speak of these two important points of the creditist doctrine, people find the solution strange, stupid, even silly. And yet, the present administration offers no solution, everyone knows that. The solution we have had, that is the application of the present monetary principles, we have to put up with it now; we are experiencing the results, the consequence: misery in the midst of abundance. Products are now being destroyed, in 1967, throughout Canada, while Canadian citizens live in slums, do not have the bare necessities, have no security at all and only have the freedom to starve while sitting on heaps of wheat. That is the present situation.
Mr. Chairman, it is all very well to laugh at solutions brought forward by others. However, let us start by considering how matters stand. For ten years and even since the end of the war-for more than ten years, for twenty-two years-we have been hearing about consumer credit. Things are getting worse all the time. It is getting worse in every field. Since the war the national debt has been increasing. The interest paid on that debt has been increasing to such an extent that this year we will pay $1,279 million in interest alone on that debt.
And we are studying here ways to help the consumers. Think of the good example the government is setting for the Canadian consumers, producers, farmers, workers, etc. And after that we are surprised to see that strikes are called, such as the dreadful one now going on within the Montreal Transportation Commission, where the workers defy the authorities, where the workers indicate that
Corporate and Consumer Affairs they are completely dissatisfied with their living conditions, and the workers are right, yes. Even if they are right, will their strike solve their problem? Of course not. I have yet to see in Canada or elsewhere in the world a strike which solved the problems of the working people.
The fate of the worker or the labour problem have never been settled by strikes. And after a strike there begins another within one, two or three years. Why? Because we wallow in a system that does not make sense and we refuse to change it. Who is paying the piper in Montreal for this strike? Is it Marcel Pepin, the president of the C.S.N? Certainly not. Mr. Chairman, it is customary, or has been so, for the governments of certain countries in the world, when they wish to set up an important but vaguely defined department to look after a broad range of domestic affairs, to designate that department as the ministry of the interior. As I listened to the Registrar General this morning it seemed to me that this might have been a better title for the new department than the one suggested-ministry of consumer affairs.
There is something about the designation "ministry of the interior" which strikes an alien note. There is a foreign connotation to it. Departments with "affairs" attached to their names are too routine. Our external affairs policy has neither changed nor accomplished anything for the last 15 years and no one expects that it will over the next 15 years. Indian affairs makes a steady but barely visible progress-we do not get excited over it very often-and as for northern affairs, we do not think about it at all.
"Department of Consumer Affairs" has, I am sure, a pleasant and satisfying sound, particularly to the government. The minister refers to the setting up of this department as "a rationalization". This, too, has a satisfying sound to it because, after all, we are rational people and we expect governments to function on a rational basis and to move only after logical thought and much discussion. But a desire for rationalization is not, of course, the reason for the formation of a department of consumer affairs. It comes about as a result of an emotional demand. There may even be some Canadians who feel that this emotional demand was that made by the housewives who protested some months ago in their anger-in many cases it was justified anger-against rising prices. The decision of the government to set up a ministry has nothing to do with anger at all but it has everything to do with fear-fear that hon. gentlemen opposite may be replaced in the very near future by the New Democratic party if they fail to move swiftly enough into the areas indicated by that party. This is the

real reason we are debating today a resolution concerning a department of consumer affairs.
No hardier contestant has ever entered the political arena than the idea of this department. The hon. member for Yukon spoke about the hearings of the committee on consumer credit and prices. He told us about the number of times this champion was dusted off by the N.D.P. and put into the ring again. Expert after expert demolished it and laid it lifeless on the floor only to find that the next day it was alive again and still around. It would not lie down though it was defeated before the committee which was looking into the whole question of consumer goods and their prices. I am sure that if this party were handling the real boxing championships, Canada would have the world championship in its possession. As I say, this idea would not lie down. Finally, the minister himself raised its hand and when we get to third reading it will be crowned as a champion, a new department, one which could have a most significant effect not only on the career of the hon. gentleman but on the government of Canada as well.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I was amazed at the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway this morning. I had expected that she would rise and simply say "Thank you, kind sir" before sitting down. But she sailed into a pseudo-attack on the very objectives which she and her colleagues have sought for so long. She had to work hard to find something to attack, because I am sure the minister has worked his hands to the bone putting forward this idea, getting it accepted by the cabinet and preparing this resolution for presentation today. But the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway found the one damned spot, which happened to be the word "corporate", and she sunk her teeth into it. I do not for a moment accuse her of biting the hand that fed her, not at all, but I would say she bit the hand that bled for her, and Mr. Chairman, who would have thought that the minister and the government had so much blood in them?

I maintain that this cannot be done logically. Once again, the main object, the main purpose that is sought is not to concentrate, or to centralize all jurisdictions within a department but rather to create a department, the function of which would be to provide the co-ordination which has now become absolutely essential and to help generally consumers to help themselves.
And now, Mr. Chairman, reverting to the argument I was trying to submit, I must say-and these are my own personal observations-that, bearing in mind what studies and surveys have been made, as well as the main objectives and the very basis of the measure, it all boils down to the fact that on the one hand, the consumer is entitled to information and, on the other hand, the government must inform the consumer.
Speaking of this question of information, if we want to appreciate the merits of the overall objectives of the public bills already entered in the order paper or of the purposes of the new department which is going to be organized, we come to the conclusion that the essential objective which should be sought and attained, in order to really help the consumers within the jurisdiction of the central government, is to educate the consumer. This, of course, will require the general co-operation of the legislatures which have this power. May I also respectfully submit that it will be necessary to teach the child, right from his early years, that is from primary school, how to protect himself in the midst of an affluent society; it will be necessary to make him familiar with the analysis of a personal budget, with sound management, so as to enable him to plan his own budget and especially to make a wise choice among all the facilities

Corporate and Consumer Affairs available to him to get this or that through finance companies, etc.
Considering this whole situation, one must readily admit that such co-ordination will have to take place within the various federal structures, in short, within all public powers.
I feel it is illusory and useless to think that the government is able, by creating a department of consumer affairs, to cure all the ills and relieve all the miseries of the people, as the hon. member for Villeneuve is blaming the government for not doing.
We are living in a free society. I respectfully submit that it is neither possible nor advisable to apply strict controls to an economy of abundance and production. The Economic Council of Canada precisely suggested that within a production first geared to our capability, production itself was the best protection for consumers, through employment, and that within that abundant production, some governmental action was essential so as to guide consumers and, in short, help them to help themselves.
Must the government seek, as a rule, to exercise a control over advertising? Is it to analyse the various means of protecting the consumer, to change the structures, even to change some jurisdictions? For instance, when my hon. friend from Villeneuve speaks about the evil effects of the system, let us say, of the finance companies-it might be the impression which was left in our province on many occasions-I say that the House of Commons is not the proper place for a full discussion of that problem, because the central government does not have the necessary powers to control the agreements entered into by corporations and individuals since it is a matter of provincial jurisdiction.
It is obviously within the legislatures that these demands must be made when we are concerned with fraud, false pretences, exchange of notes and promissory notes, contract transfer or contract financing. All these, except the Bills of Exchange Act, are under provincial jurisdiction and obviously, whatever the good will of the central government may be, it is necessarily up to the provinces to apply their own legislation in this field.
The hon. member for Yukon was here a minute ago. Now he was suggesting, on the one hand, the creation of an interdepartmental committee but, on the other hand, he seemed to blame the government for not strictly following the proposals of the Economic Council of Canada which on page 22 recommends the creation of a department of

I once made a personal analysis of an act -as a lawyer, of course, I had the opportunity to practice-for instance, the Bills of Exchange Act for which the central power is responsible. This would provide an opportunity to discuss in committee the provisions of the bill, to call witnesses, examine the purposes of the bill and understand it in detail. I sometimes wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether we are not getting away from the real search for the answers to some of the problems which so plague us today. The consumers of this country have problems; there is no question about that. I do not think that legislation of this kind will provide the answers to these problems. I do not think it will provide even a very small part of the answers. I do not believe the consumers of Canada will sleep any more soundly after this legislation is passed and steps taken to implement it than they did before, in spite of the very careful administration that I am sure the legislation will receive from the minister.
There is a fallacy in the minds of governments and many people that by passing legislation of this kind, by moving to create new departments and government agencies, we can solve problems. We can no more solve problems in this way than we can by repeating cliches when talking about them. The difficulty is that there are just not enough of the right things, produced in the right way and at the right place, to consume. I believe it is more a matter of production than consumption. I believe my hon. friends to my left would agree that during the war one of the most important departments created in this country was the Department of Defence Production. That department was created to firmly, and if necessary even ruthlessly and brutally, brush aside all the conventions, mores, usages and customs of people engaged in the business of production and direct and divert the production of the country to a more specific purpose.
In the light of what was said by the Economic Council of Canada I do not believe the creation of this new department will serve the necessary purpose. There is no question that this is what affects us. As I said the other day, you can tax for the purpose of redistributing wealth but all it does is to consume wealth. It does not produce one single item more of wealth. Wealth is produced only by the application of labour to natural resources.

Here we may have to look at the application of this legislation with regard to the future course of consumers and of production in this country. We may have to examine the extent to which there exists a sufficiently broad base under our constitutional system on which to found a valid and workable system to deal with combines and restrictive trade practices and misleading advertising.

Then there is the question of taxes. Much has been said in the house about the production tax. One of the problems which faces consumers today is the limitation on the production of goods and services which they need as a result of the inadequate and obsolete system of taxation which prevails. That does not mean that I support the Carter commission.
Let me give an illustration of a matter which may not be completely under federal jurisdiction. One of the problems with which we have been dealing here is housing. To what extent does taxation affect the problem of housing and the availability of housing? I can recall the first house I built 35 or 38 years ago. At that time I paid $30 for three lots and about $2,500 for the house. When I came back from overseas in 1946 I paid $600 for a lot and about $8,000 or $9,000 for the house. What does one have to pay today in the large metropolitan centres and in most of the urban areas in Canada? Anywhere from $6,000 to $10,000 or $12,000 for a lot and from $15,000 to $18,000 for a house.
These are problems which an inadequate system of taxation has made possible. Under the present system of municipal or provincial taxation improvements on land are taxed as well as the land itself. If only the land were taxed this would make available

The taxation system which would be required to do this might prove to be one of the solutions to the housing problem. I am not suggesting, of course, that the federal government can do this, although it can certainly exert some pressure in this direction. What I wish to say is that this problem affects not only the consumers but also affects the question of production, the availability of products, of land, of services and of commodities at a range in price that Canadians can meet and in quantities they require.
Then there is the question of tariffs in international trade. How can we speak about doing things for the consumer when we have a tariff system which imposes burdens and restraints on the consumer? The picture looks pretty black from here. I was reading today a press dispatch from Washington. A joint resolution is being introduced there by a Republican and a Democratic senator to seek the approval of Congress to impose restrictions upon the import of steel and steel products into the United States. A trend has developed in the United States and in other countries which is very ominous in the light of the situation which brought about the great depression of many years ago. If there ever was a country which must flourish and whose people would be the beneficiaries by reason of a system of freer trade, it is Canada. This is one of the areas in which the energies of the government should be concentrated in an effort to help the consumers.

I think the best way of understanding what this resolution proposes is to read it:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a department of corporate and consumer affairs; to provide for the appointment of a minister and a deputy minister and for their duties and powers; to provide that the governor in council may establish a consumer advisory council and other bodies to assist the minister and for the remuneration and expenses of the members thereof; and to provide for certain other matters related or incidental thereto.
Is there a problem? After having listened to members of this house for nearly two years, I am sure there is a problem in connection with consumer affairs. First, there is the high cost of living which everybody has been denouncing. Another aspect of the problem is easily observed in the kind of social disorder we are experiencing now in connection with the escalation of strikes. There is a new attitude on the part of strikers. In the past they used to strike peacefully but now they appear to be revolutionists. Their general attitude, for instance, is one of disregard for the requisites of the laws of this country. This is a dangerous attitude, I feel, but it results from the exasperation experienced by most of our people in connection with the rising cost of living. Certainly there is a problem. The point at which we disagree is when we try to find a solution to this problem.
I want to make some comments on another matter which is not really related to this subject. There are some members of the house to whom I like to listen because every time I listen to them I learn a little from their logic and the way they express themselves. These members belong to all parties but one I relish listening to is the hon. member for Peace River, who just spoke. He made one remark with which I agree, that in this country there is a state of emergency which requires drastic action by the government.
I am sure that the parliamentary secretary to the minister, who has the famous city of Montmorency in his riding, knows what he is saying when he speaks on constitutional matters. He says it is not the business of the federal government to fix prices. I believe, however, that means can be found for getting together with the provinces to try to find a way of controlling prices which are always rising and are causing desperation amongst our population. I am one of those who believe we have a real emergency. As proof of that statement I mention the escalation of strikes and the revolutionary attitude one notices on the part of delegations coming to this parliament to protest against what they term the
October 13, 1967

inadequacy of government measures to cope with this problem.
Is there a better solution than the one proposed by the government? There may be. I am sure there may be as good a solution, perhaps even a better one, but who can swear that he is infallible? What counts, I believe, is that we do something and that we do it as fast as possible. This is one solution, and although it may not be as drastic as I would have liked I believe that the minister who will be in charge of this department will have everything he needs to make a success of this enterprise. He is dynamic and openminded. I am sure that of the candidates to head this department he is one who is well prepared to do a good job.
However, if he does not do a good job he will And that the opposition will be watching him closely. They will take every opportunity to offer him suggestions to help make a success of this endeavour to cope with the high cost of living and the problems of consumers. In addition to the high cost of living, there is the problem of advertising abuses, false representations. I understand, of course, that some members of the house prefer the complete socialization of our economy, the complete control of our economy. I would not be against that in principle but we might not be ready for such action now.
I suppose the good service that the New Democratic party renders to this country lies in the fact that their suggestions may be three or four years ahead of time. When the time is ripe governments, Conservative and Liberal, take these ideas and translate them in the way they understand them. Even if our friends in the New Democratic party do not have the advantage of forming a government, they are really rendering a good service to this country by their suggestions for the improvement of the lot of all Canadians.
I should like to mention now a special category of consumers who are the victims of some brainwashing. They are not really protected as they should be. Before going any further I should apologize, Mr. Chairman, and warn you that I may not be completely in order when I try to prove that these consumers consume something that is not material but has a lot of influence. I refer to the voters of this country. They are the victims of candidates or parties that have a lot of money with which to wage their campaigns. These candidates or parties can buy pages of advertising in the newspapers and can buy a lot of time on television and radio. They organize a real
Corporate and Consumer Affairs brainwashing. The result in some ridings often is that somebody is elected who is not well prepared to do the job, who has no experience and is only a partisan.
I want to put this as gently as I can, Mr. Chairman. I will say that there is none of these people in this house at the present time. However, this is something that can happen occasionally. I do not believe we should permit in our democracy the buying of voters with a lot of advertising. You can buy a lot of advertising when you have millionaires backing you. They will give you the money needed to do the brainwashing and then come here and lobby to influence the legislation the government presents. I believe I have given an example of consumers who are abused by too much advertising. I know the minister has good intentions but he should exert all his influence toward reforming our electoral laws, and the sooner the better. In this way we will have elections in which men will be pitted against men and not money against men which may result in the election of a man who lacks experience. We have seen a lot of exaggeration, a lot of humbug written not only to sell goods but to sell candidates who are not well prepared to represent the people of this country. This is an example of consumers being abused and they should be looked after.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I merely want to say that I believe this resolution should be adopted. I believe there is a sincere effort being made to improve the lot of the Canadian people. It might not be the best effort but it is at least sincere, and I am ready to vote for such efforts at any time. As I say, Mr. Chairman, I am sure the minister is well prepared to do a good job and I am also sure that the opposition will be watching so closely that he will not be allowed to make even the smallest mistake.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this being the resolution stage of the proceedings on this measure I intend to be very brief and mention only a few points that I want to put on the record. First of all I want to congratulate the government on introducing this resolution and taking the decision to establish the department of corporate and consumer affairs envisaged by the resolution. To the minister who will be taking over that new position very soon I wish success and good wishes as minister of corporate and consumer affairs.
I think the decision to set up this department comes in large measure from the
October 13, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs recommendations of the joint Senate-House of Commons committee on consumer credit and consumer prices which sat all last year. I think the members of that committee, all of whom worked so hard, can take a good deal of pride in the resolution that is before the house today as well as a good deal of pride in the legislation which will be introduced into the house. The joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons recommended in its interim report of December 16, and again in its final report of May 8, that a department of consumer affairs be established to concentrate on the protection of the Canadian consumer.
There has been much discussion here this afternoon about what was said by the Economic Council of Canada in its report about consumer affairs and the Department of the Registrar General, and it seems to me important to bear in mind one statement of the Economic Council which is to be found on page 21:
It is clear that there will be timely implementation of appropriate policies in the field of consumer affairs only if informed spokesmen for consumers are present to participate in the early stages of the government's consideration of these matters.
In my view, Mr. Chairman, in spite of the mechanics that the economic council may have put forward later in its report, this is an indication that the Economic Council of Canada certainly accepted the premise that there must be in cabinet and in government somebody to speak out on behalf of consumers. That, of course, was the basis of the joint committee's recommendation, both in its interim and in its final report. They indicated that the time had now come when there should be a person of cabinet rank sitting in cabinet and participating in government decisions who would represent and act as spokesman for the Canadian consumer.
If there should be some conflict between the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada and the recommendations of the joint Senate-House of Commons committee, my support will go to the recommendations of the joint committee. In this regard I should like to inform the hon. member for Peace River, who seemed to place such reliance on the views of the Economic Council of Canada, that the joint committee which recommended this department consisted of 36 members drawn from all walks of life in Canada. I think they formed a fair representation of Canadian opinion, and they came to their recommendations after hearing witnesses representing business, trade associations, universities, consumer groups and the

public generally. The evidence the committee heard was given by a very broad cross-section of Canadian public opinion. At the conclusion of this very exhaustive evidence this committee, composed of members from all parties in the house, recommended the establishment of this department.

speechtext:
I do not know, but I want to say something toward the end of my remarks about the consumers advisory council.
Much was said this morning by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, to whom I listened with interest, about her great disappointment that this department is going to be called the department of corporate and consumer affairs. May I, with respect, suggest to the hon. lady that this criticism is something of a red herring. She expressed disappointment that the recommendations of the committee, which were simply and solely for a department of consumer affairs, were not being implemented but that instead we were going to have a department of corporate and consumer affairs.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, the committee was solely concerned, and its terms of reference were solely concerned, with consumer affairs. Therefore its recommendations dealt solely with the establishment of a department of consumer affairs. Second, and more importantly, if the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway will review, as I am sure she has, some of the recommendations of the joint committee she will see there were recommendations dealing with public disclosure in regard to corporations and with the whole area of corporate law. She will also see there were many observations and recommendations dealing with concentration in the food industry and in other industries. She will see there were observations and recommendations dealing with, for example, unfair trade practices. All of these were matters dealt with by the joint committee. All of them are now matters
October 13, 1967	COMMONS
that will be falling under the jurisdiction of the department of corporate and consumer affairs, and I submit they fall logically within this same department.
Let us consider bankruptcy for a moment, Mr. Chairman, which is also a matter over which the Registrar General has responsibility and over which the new minister and his department will have responsibility. It seems to me that unless our bankruptcy laws are efficiently and effectively administered no one loses but the consumer because the ultimate cost of bankruptcy has to be borne by the buying public. Therefore it seems to me logical to put such matters as combines, corporations, securities, bankruptcies and so on under the same jurisdiction as matters relating to consumer affairs. As I say, unless these respective pieces of financial legislation are properly administered no one but the consumer himself will suffer hurt.
In addition, it seems to me there should be a logical, co-ordinated and consistent approach to corporate and securities legislation and to matters affecting financial institutions in the same way as there is to what I call the more narrow, simple consumer protection matters. Therefore, to criticize the government for combining these two functions seems to me something of a red herring indeed.
This being the resolution stage, Mr. Chairman, I have not, of course, seen the legislation which will be introduced on passage of the resolution. Nevertheless I am hopeful that it is sufficiently strong enough to deal with the recommendations that the joint committee made and sufficiently strong enough to be able to carry those recommendations forward.
I now want to say a word about consumer protection. It seems to me that in spite of what is being said in this house today against the establishment of a department of consumer affairs and even by the most violent opponent-and there are some in the country-of a department of consumer affairs, this government or any other government has a duty, one which has often been recognized, to protect members of the public against hazards to health or safety or against fraud or deception. Of course, both at the federal level and provincial levels, a number of pieces of legislation have been passed with that duty or obligation in mind, namely, legislation which does protect people against hazards to health or safety or against fraud.

Corporate and Consumer Affairs [DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I refer, for example, to certain sections of the Criminal Code which while under the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice are actually administered by the ten provincial attorneys general; to the Food and Drugs Act administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare; to the Agricultural Products Standards Act, administered by the Department of Agriculture; and to the Weights and Measures Act administered by the Department of Trade and Commerce, to name only a few. Without in any way reflecting on either the ability or the conscientiousness of the civil servants operating these acts I think it can be clearly shown that because of this hodgepodge of legislative and administrative responsibilities and duties there is a lack of co-ordination between one administration and another. All the evidence before the joint committee went to show that this was the case. Certainly the report of the economic council in connection with consumer affairs points out that there is a great lack of co-ordination in the administration of the various acts now in force designed to protect consumers.
Without attempting to discuss in detail legislation covering, for example, automobile safety, or the flammability of textiles, which are areas where legislation may be required, it seems to me eminently sensible that there should be a much greater degree of co-ordination of the existing statutes, and this kind of organization could best be achieved through setting up a department of corporate and consumer affairs.
Much has been said in this house recently about voluntary restraint, voluntary action and voluntary codes of ethics. I wish to express a caveat. While much can be done as a result of industry voluntarily restraining itself by adopting codes of ethics and the like, I believe we would be making a mistake if we thought this was the best means by which the public could be protected. We in this house should not be lulled into thinking that voluntary action can be relied upon to solve the problems of consumer protection. The submission of the Better Business Bureaux which made representations to our committee could be summed up, it seems to me, by the words: "Leave us alone and we will protect the consumer." Without in any way reflecting on the work the bureaux have done across Canada-and they have done excellent work -there are still consumers who need protection; there are still consumers who are being
October 13, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs gypped by unscrupulous operators, and I think it can be shown time and time again that there are occasions when it is necessary for government to intervene.
I should like to give two examples. The first has to do with the Association of Canadian Chemical Specialty Manufacturers. This is made up of companies which manufacture some of the household cleaning solvents and solutions we use domestically. This association has drawn up a code of ethics, a very good code which provides for the proper labelling of the goods they produce, indicating which substances are dangerous and listing antidotes to be used should they be taken internally by young children, and so on. Members of this industry deserve thanks and credit for acting in this responsible and socially conscious way. The flaw is that nonmembers of the association do not need to comply with the code and, as a result, there are available in our stores household chemicals and cleaners which, in fact, are not properly labelled with appropriate warnings where necessary. Thus, while voluntary action is successful to the extent that those who agree with the code comply with it, there are unfortunately still those who refuse to comply with such provisions.
Let me offer another example. A man came to me a while ago and accused me of supporting a government which was keeping him up at nights. He brought me a number of cans of processed meat from various countries including New Zealand, Denmark, Australia, the United States and Canada. He told me that if he bought a can of meat from New Zealand, from Denmark or from Great Britain he knew from the label what was contained in the can. This was important because his son was an allergenic who could eat only certain types of meat, and if the food was not chosen correctly he was kept awake all night. Mr. Chairman, I have not noticed the meat packing industry in those other countries I have mentioned going out of business because they were required to state on the labels of these cans exactly what was contained inside the cans. It seems to me a national disgrace that here in Canada when we buy processed meat in a supermarket we should have no idea whether it contains beef or pork or liver or heart_

Or horsemeat. This man argued that here in Canada we are surely sophisticated enough to require manufacturers to state on their labels exactly what is contained in their product. It seems to me

that for the sake of allergenies there is immediate need for a minister to assure that attention is given to the proper labelling of food, cosmetics, and other products.
As I promised the hon. member for Peace River, I will say a word about the consumer advisory committee. The resolution proposes the establishment of such a committee, and it seems to me it would be a useful and worthwhile body to give advice to the minister, as suggested by the Economic Council of Canada. It will consist of possibly 15 persons drawn from various walks of life in Canada-representatives of consumer groups, merchandisers, academics, businessmen and so on. The presence of this advisory committee concentrating on consumer affairs would assure that the government was responsive to the needs of the country and that its actions were in line with the demands both of the consumers and of the economy.
There are two questions which I hope the advisory committee will take under study right away; they are mentioned briefly in one of the reports of our joint committee. First, there is the question of taxes and tariffs which was referred to by the hon. member for Peace River. The committee report referred to the incidence of taxes and tariffs on the prices of goods to the consumer, and I believe the consumer advisory committee would do well to commission some studies along this line to find out how some of the costs to the consumer might be relieved. We shall all of course have to continue paying taxes, but I think it can be shown that some taxes have a greater impact on prices than others.

I think that would be a very worth-while study by the committee. Also, there are some commodities on which we have tariffs and I can find no logical basis for tariffs being on them. For instance, I see no reason why Canada imposes tariffs on bananas. I am not aware of any Canadian banana crop that needs protection, yet we have a tariff on bananas.

I think the consumer advisory committee should examine the existing list of tariffs in order to eliminate those which are providing no measure of protection. All they are doing is upping costs to the Canadian consumer. The committee should give further study to the whole question of tariffs. It seems to me there are many logical reasons, as pointed out by the hon. member for Peace River, why we in Canada will be better off if we have the freest possible trade and the lowest possible level of tariffs. This would give encouragement to industry to specialize and improve, thus putting it in a competitive position in international trade.
It can certainly be shown that, the lower tariffs are, the better off are consumers when they go to the supermarkets and spend their dollars. If we in Canada can reduce our tariffs we will effect considerable saving to the purchasing public. Last night I was delighted to read a speculative article in the Financial Post indicating that even Ontario manufacturers are beginning to see the benefit to Canada and themselves of lower tariffs and free trade. I would hope that article is correct and that the Ontario manufacturers, who traditionally have been opposed to free trade, will reverse their position and support those of us who believe in low tariffs and free trade. This is one aspect of protection that the consumer advisory committee could look into immediately on its formation.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I am going to be brief in my observations at the resolution stage of the legislation. I am delighted the government has decided to establish a department of consumer affairs. I wish it well. I look forward to seeing the bill, and I hope its provisions will be strong enough to implement the recommendations we made in our joint committee.

These

Corporate and Consumer Affairs problems are of great magnitude. The first problem concerns the highest cost of living ever experienced in the history of Canada. I suppose that is what the minister had in mind when he sponsored this resolution.
The second problem is that Canada today is facing a very serious financial crisis. This crisis is being somewhat hidden from the Canadian people because the Minister of Finance not only has the name Sharp but he has a sharp mind and a sharp way of being able to cover up the crisis the Canadian people are now experiencing, but of which they will have full knowledge in the very near future.
In the introduction to my remarks I think it would be good to see what the resolution has to say. We have not got the bill which will follow, and so it is difficult to criticize that. Therefore I must speak in reference to the principles involved. The resolution says that -
-it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a department of corporate and consumer
affairs-

-to provide for the appointment of a minister and a deputy minister and for their duties and powers; to provide that the governor in council may establish a consumer advisory council and other bodies to assist the minister-

It is not so long ago that the House of Commons heard from the government that it was changing the nature of the Economic Council of Canada. This council was to be the advisory body that would advise the government. I wonder whether the minister can tell us-probably at another stage of the debate he will-when the economic council fell out of favour with the government. Its members were his appointments, or his government's appointments. The members of the council were to be the great men who would guide the government, who would advise how to control the cost of living, and how to control the large government bureaucracy from extending like an octopus into every facet of Canadian life.
What did that council say, and what advice has it given the minister and the government? This advice has already been read into

Corporate and Consumer Affairs the record, but I think this might be a good time to review it because alter listening to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard one would almost think that this was the beginning of a new era to bring down the cost of living, control it, and do something about the financial crisis the nation is facing. Let us see what the economic council said. At page 20 of its interim report it said:
In view of the wide scope of consumer interests-
Consumers are sure interested because on orders of the day the Minister of Finance said he went to a store and found the prices were going down. He must have been shopping in a different store from that used by any other Canadian. He is unique in that regard; he has his own monopoly in his own private store. The report continues:
In view of the wide scope of consumer interests and the many departments which are engaged in activities affecting consumers, there is no possibility of concentrating all these activities in a single department, nor would it be desirable to try to do so.
That was the advice of the wise men appointed by the government to advise it. But the moment these wise men measured up to their responsibilities as economic statesmen and advised the government of the trend it has been taking, a decision was taken to change the nature of the economic council.
Before I sit down I am going to endeavour to prove, and I think I will prove, that the government is partly, if not totally, responsible for the high cost of living. It is certainly responsible for government spending. I recall the days during the 1963 election when Liberals used to get on platforms and talk about the deficits incurred by the Conservative government. They were just like infants, babies in prams, compared to the deficits of today. If one reads the full report made by the economic council he will see that government costs in Canada have gone up 25 per cent more than in the United States, even though the United States is fighting a war in Viet Nam.
But let me return to the point I was making, that it was the government which appointed these wise men. Now it is throwing out the same wise men saying, "We are politicians, we know better. We will set up another council. We will line up Liberals. This time we want to make sure they are real Liberals. The other fellows may have been Grits. They have put us in an intolerable position with the public and we may be defeated in the next election. So we will set up another body to assist us, to advise us."
