Yes, "Tell us nicer things." That is absolutely correct. But here we have the economic council saying it cannot be done.
Let us talk about the high cost of living for a few minutes. 1 have always been one of those who believe that not only do we have a crisis in this nation at a time of war, but there are also times when we have other crises that are just as severe in the sense of survival-economic crises. I know that some of my hon. friends to my left will agree with me on this.
The courts have interpreted the constitution-and I know the minister appreciates this line of the law-to mean that in times of crisis, "peace, order and good government", to use the phrase which appears in the B.N.A. Act, override property and civil rights, and so the government can bring in controls such as we had during war. But there is another line of thought which holds that an economic crisis is comparable to a time of war, even though the state is not being threatened by a foreign power. This line of thought holds that in such case the federal government has authority to control prices, to control wages and to control profits. If the government had some real spunk it would bring in regulations to control those things which are causing the cost of living to spiral.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
For a solid year and a half I have asked the Prime Minister where the Woods report is, the report which has reference to the relationship between management and labour. This session he told me, as he did last session, that it was very important. He said that they would be rushing it in, in two or three weeks. I do not know what the finding of the Woods report will be, but soon some government some time-not these people, some hope-will have to measure up to its responsibility to this nation in reference to the labour-management relationship, because you cannot have a Pearson formula of 30 per cent, have it duplicated the next year in respect of the S.I.U., have costs spiralling and everything going up and expect to set up a department which will control prices.
I have not seen the bill, but if I had to vote at this moment I would probably vote in favour of it because any little bit is better than nothing. But the government is not even scratching the surface of this problem. This is strictly window dressing to try to show the Canadian people that they are going to do
October 13, 1967	COMMONS
something about the cost of living. What has caused the costs to rise so quickly? No government has been such a free spender as has this government. Take a look at the budget of 1963 and the budget of 1966. When you do that, you will see what has happened. We have heard the boloney-we in western Canada call it boloney-that the great Minister of Finance has pared off $700 million. This is sophistry. We know what he is doing. This always has happened in the past. The minister comes in and presents his estimates. Trimming always takes place. But they have not trimmed anything off the estimates which actually gets into the budget. They just blow up a great big piece of propaganda.
If these wise ministers, who they believe are wiser than the members of the economic council, had trimmed their estimates before they came in or, to put it the other way, had enlarged them, the minister could say that they have saved the Canadian people $2 billion or $3 billion. This is straight sophistry. When we came back with a new leader we were organized and we were doing our homework, but they called us the same old gang. This might bring headlines; but I say to them that the "same old gang" is running the Liberal party.
Let us look at the headline in the Toronto Daily Star of October 5, 1967. I could not say that this paper is unfriendly to the Liberals. If it is, then this is something new, because it says, "Stop wage-price climb or I'll up taxes-Sharp". Do you know what Sharp said? I do not know what he said to the members of the cabinet, and I should like to hear what he said to my friend the young minister who said, "free this and free that". He mentioned 15 free items when he appeared on T.Y. He thought everything would be free. Sharp told the Canadian people that if they do not behave themselves and stop doing this, that or the other thing, if they do not stop spending money, the government will increase taxes and bring on unemployment. Then they will let the Tories come in, so that they again can say that a Conservative government brings in hard times, as it was alleged to have done in 1957.

When the minister goes into cabinet I wish he would say, "We will cut back on government spending". But what is he actually doing today? He says he is going to set up a new department, which basically is only going to investigate, take a look, and obtain some information.
We might take the example of the Department of Industry. It started with a little group, and all of a sudden it is large. It is no wonder that the estimates have gone up. This is the growth of bureaucracy. This country is over-governed. We have more people working for the government than has any nation in the world. The new minister says that we need another department because we have a problem and must set up another department through which to funnel information. I do not think the minister believes that what he is doing today will control the high cost of living. He must start right now to cut down on government expenditure and stop threatening the people with increased taxes.
What is wrong with the economy? My friend from Assiniboia mentioned wheat. In June we heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce say that the price of wheat would be set at 21 cents a bushel more. They had an agreement and all they had to do was have it ratified in the parliamentary institutions of the 52 countries; but that evening when he reported he never said that the agreement had lapsed. The United States then dumped

So, we know that not a dollar will be paid out of the treasury. As I said before and as I say now we were until recently the chief wheat exporting nation of the world. I think it is fair to say that these sales took place under the Conservative and Liberal governments because the markets were opened by the Conservative government. I hope that later in this debate the minister will tell us precisely and definitively just what that line is.
As far as public health or safety are concerned, will the minister take some action with regard to air pollution? Will he take some action against the large corporations in this country which with impunity are pouring all manner of pollution into the air and waters of Canada? I was disturbed when I saw the interim report of the council on consumer affairs and the Department of the Registrar General because I have always had respect for the Economic Council of Canada and its personnel, many of whom are known to me personally. But this report seemed to be nothing short of a disgrace. The council asks questions which it does not answer. Let us consider some of them, for instance the following one which appears on page 7 of the report:
The following questions, for example, need to be answered before it can be known whether higher standards of living are likely to result from an increase in output:
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands).!

-What form has the increase in output taken?
Would the consumers have preferred something else?
Did consumers have sufficient information to make informed choices? Could the same products have been made available at lower prices?
-Supposing the consumer has bought what he wants, how well does the article function in use? What is its frequency-of-repair record? Does it expose the user to unnecessary hazards?
Such questions indicate that the performance of the economy cannot be judged exclusively by the behaviour of total output and income.
Having asked these questions the council gives no answer whatsoever. Instead, on page 8 of the report it goes on to make statements which I think are open to very serious doubt, such as the following one:
...''the interests of the consumer, in the light of the government's long-term economic objectives", are only served to the degree that the growing productive capabilities of the economy are in fact converted into improvements in living standards.
Whose living standards are they referring to?
The major responsibility-
This is something that I am afraid the minister has swallowed hook, line and sinker.
[DOT]-for seeing that an efficient conversion of this kind takes place devolves in our society upon business and consumers themselves. Obviously the minister and his colleague, the Minister of Finance, took this as their guide line of action and really believe that we can, in the present modem age, leave to business and to consumers these decisions as to the nature of our society. I suggest to the minister, who is a young man, who will be in politics long after I am dead, and who has a tremendous opportunity, that he should realize that today in Canada the government is facing a challenge created by modem technology which makes a fool of all conventional wisdom, that the addiction of this government and all the governments we have had to date to a devotion to the free enterprise system and to the glories of profit-making are irrelevant in the modern age.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to say a few words on this proposed resolution.
According to the resolution, a new department is to be established, whose purpose and duty it will be to balance our economy so that consumer goods can be disposed of and the people can enjoy them.
I doubt that the creation of a new department will cure all our economic ills. Our economy is completely out of balance and the creation of several departments before this one has not succeeded in boosting the economy of our country. The more the present system is applied, the more it throws our economy out of balance and, as a solution, the creation of new departments is suggested. By creating new departments you increase the cost of the products and right away you will have to increase taxes immediately to meet the expenditures of that new department. One knows how much it costs the nation to administer a department. There are some whose administration costs almost 60 per cent of their budget. There are others that probably spend even more. The department of corporate and consumer affairs which will be set up will not escape all that. Like the others, it will have to open new offices, put up new buildings, hire a great number of bureaucrats and pay them large salaries, and all that costs the nation a lot of money.
I think that, at the present time, we have enough departments. I do not think that it is by the creation of a new department that we
DEBATES	3101.
Corporate and Consumer Affairs will add to the purchasing power of consumers. If a department makes a few practical suggestions in order to increase the purchasing power of consumers, the general economy will object and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) will say that revenues are not sufficient.
I do not think that it is a practical solution. The best one is still to increase the purchasing power of the consumers through the existing departments. The Department of Finance would have to deal mainly with this situation since it is the one responsible. There is no consumer credit and the consumers have no money, no purchasing power, the goods remain in storage and in the stores, and the citizens are further deprived of them.
Then, Mr. Chairman, if we put more buying power in the consumers' hands, we can conclude with certainty that production will not be found wanting in Canada. Canadian production is financed to the tune of about 75 per cent and even at that, we have piled up surpluses. Production is finance but not consumption.
The buying power which is distributed through work and capital, is not sufficient to put in the hands of every individual, of the unemployed, of those who do not have buying power through capital assets or work, what is needed to provide the necessities of life. We must put in the hands of consumers adequate buying power if we want to consume our products.
Our surplus production stood at $18 billion in 1966-67 and exceeded $15 billion in 196566. We have had surplus goods ever since the end of the war, since 1945. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, if our surplus production is so high, the problem is not with production, because it has already been settled.
No problems either with regard to transportation. Why is transportation so costly? Because everything related to transportation is so heavily taxed: trucks, tires, gas, and this makes for an increased cost of living.
I wonder what the new department of consumer affairs will do in all this. Will it reduce transportation costs? Will it reduce interest rates? Will it reduce income and other taxes so as to lower the cost price of goods and enable consumers to purchase a certain amount of goods with the same dollar?
So, Mr. Chairman, I hardly think that this department will perform miracles and I feel that creating such a department is a pipe dream.
October 13, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
I have here a report showing that almost all citizens, public bodies or associations that have presented briefs have come to the conclusion that we need a new department of consumers.
The same report also indicates that there are other citizens who also have made studies and all kinds of suggestions. In fact, some of them are very practical. For instance, the Maritime Co-operative Council of Moncton, New Brunswick stated, as reported on page 3111, that:
For the purposes of this presentation, we say there are two fields of credit: purchase of merchandise on credit and the borrowing of direct purchasing power. We believe that consumers are being exploited in both these fields.
That is what we have been saying and repeating for a long time, Mr. Chairman. I continue:
Not so many years ago, individuals tried not to become indebted particularly for the purchase of merchandise. Thus, those who could lend money realized that individuals did not then constitute a very good market but that their institutions could be used to advantage in that area. As a result, credit was built up in all public institutions such as schools, cities, municipalities, provinces, the Dominion, etc. and all that is needed is to look at the interest charges on the national debt which now exceed 1 billion dollars yearly (see Appendix 1) to understand the cost the consumer must meet through all kinds of taxes collected at the source or on the price of merchandise, the price of labour or other corresponding factors.
It was stated that the consumers had been opposed to borrowing, but in the last few years it seems that the situation has changed, in that consumer credit has reached what we consider to be an alarming level where debts amount to several billions of dollars. The related credit charges push up prices and, incidentally, further depreciate the dollar and cause inflation.
I wonder what the departments are going to do about inflation and deflation. Now, deflation is never discussed because it only affects the small fry, the poor; it is not worthwhile discussing it. But inflation is discussed, because it affects everyone.
And now, back to the quotation:
Federal legislation providing for the complete disclosure to purchasers and borrowers of interest rates and other charges on loans. (Legislation to bring loans out in the open.)
Role of money or credit.
In commerce, money or credit should help the flow of goods or services. It should not be controlled as a basic material. Even today, chartered banks are rather accounting institutions which control the creation of the monetary mass or credit, as if it were a raw matrial having a tremendous influence on the world of business, and they can set interest rates. The cost of money or credit should not exceed that of accounting, but when money or credit are controlled as one would a raw material, it is used to brake or stimulate
rMr. Latulippe.]
the flow of goods according to the wishes of those who control it, with a view to making profits and not solely to serve business.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
We have been talking about those things for so long that at least today we feel some support in the claims we have made for years. Therefore, I continue:
Royal commission on banking and finance.
The report of the royal commission on banking and finance explained on page 105 how the banks create the money supply or credit. After explaining how the Bank of Canada authorizes the chartered banks to create more money or more credit, the report of the royal commission continues with this statement.
This is taken from the report, Mr. Chairman, the words are not mine.
Thus if the first bank finds its cash increased by $8 million by the initial Bank of Canada purchase from one of its customers and grants a loan of $7 million to a customer who spends it on additional supplies, the suppliers will re-deposit these funds in other banks which will in turn find themselves with extra cash with which to add to their assets. At this point, the banks as a group will find that their deposits have risen by $15 million-$8 million from the original security purchase and $7 million from the proceeds of the loan-but their cash has increased by $8 million. Since their cash ratio is still higher than it need be, this process of expansion will continue, only coming to a halt, all other things being equal, when the liabilities of the banking system have increased by $100 million. At this point the statutory cash ratio of 8 per cent has been restored and any further expansion would bring the ratio below the requirement.
It is to be noted that the requirement in regard to the 8 per cent reserve with the Bank of Canada has been reduced to 7 per cent shortly after, which in fact has empowered the chartered banks to increase credit to that extent on the basis of their deposit with the Bank of Canada. It should be remembered that interest is being collected on these amounts entered in their books as loans.
That the Bank of Canada have greater control of the production and distribution of necessary credit (money).
Financing through cooperatives.
A major solution available to consumers who wish to solve their financing problem or succeed in paying expenditures they must incur could be and in fact already is, the creation of cooperative financial institutions.
Such institutions could include among others the caisses populaires (credit unions), the credit cooperatives, the cooperative insurance companies and cooperative trust companies.
There is nothing magical about all this. In the case of the caisses populaires, the members cannot borrow more than what is deposited as savings, which is not the case for banks. A number of people invariably manage to save up money, and these savings are then available at a reasonable
October 13. 1967

interest to those who need them. In every cooperative financial institution of this kind, those who contributed to the build-up of capital retain only a limited control on its use, whereas other institutions use it for profit and exploitation. This type of activity and organization, which helps its members (users or consumers) to save up money, should be encouraged by the joint committee and benefit from government support.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I ask myself again, what will the department of consumer affairs do in all this? What will it settle in all this?
When the Conservatives, Liberals and N.D.P. members voted for the increase in interest rates, they did everything possible to give high finance all the necessary powers for further exploitation of the people.
When we moved amendments to the Bank Act for the purpose of freezing interest rates at 6 per cent, most members in all parties, old and new, voted against them, then they call themselves the defenders of the people. On the contrary, they are the defenders of high finance, of hypocrisy, that is what they are, the members of every other party in this house. No other member, except us, called for any financial readjustment. It is imperative that our economy regain its balance, yet this will never be achieved by continuing to allow economic imbalance, by allowing higher cost of living in every economic sector, by maintaining the same attitude in the fields of strikes, wage increases, taxes, fiscal levies and interest rates. These members allowed all that and they claim to be the defenders of the people; as Our Lord said, they are only hypocrites, white sepulchres.
I do not want to dwell longer on that subject, Mr. Chairman. The minister knows and all the members know that things are going badly. Nobody proposes solutions except to try this and that; they try all sorts of things, which gets them nowhere, instead of balancing the wheels of the economic mechanism. We have a big wheel and a small wheel on the economic chariot, so that the system turns in a circle. Instead of using two wheels of the same size to attain the objective, they enjoy loading the chariot, unloading it and doing all kinds of repairs except changing the small wheel which should be balanced with the other, so that the system might go straight and balance the economy.
The economy is always kept unbalanced and no one wants to make the necessary adjustments to the economic wheel so that it will turn in the right direction and give our economy a balance which might satisfy every Canadian.

Corporate and Consumer Affairs
In our country there are people who make money and there are some who live by their work and their capital. There are 7,400,000 citizens who receive an income from their work and their capital, but there are also 13 million citizens who have no income from their work or their capital but who are taxed and have to pay the same taxes as all the others. On the other hand, out of those 7,-
400,000	citizens who derive an income from their capital or their work, 2,400,000 do not earn enough to pay income tax.
So what is that new department of consumer credit going to do about those problems? Is it going to plant potatoes, to grow potatoes? Is it going to distribute the produce of the land? No. The land will continue to produce. No one worries about tomorrow, to the extent that production is not lacking.
But if, as I said a while ago, we were to finance 100 per cent of our whole production, all the means of production, we could double it: it would jump from $62 billion to $124 billion.
This would be possible in Canada since, at the present time, one third of the population, of the working class, is not working; it could produce, help production whereas, now, it is unemployed and lives at someone else's expense.
They steal from those who work to give to those who do nothing.
So, Mr. Chairman, we have a complete lack of balance, to the point that the worker is as poor as the unemployed. The parasite living off society gets as much as the worker, because the latter sees his pay dwindle on account of income tax and the various other taxes deducted from his salary.
With all those association and union dues, the various taxes deducted from his pay, the worker is as poor as the one receiving social assistance.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
There is a deplorable imbalance that should be corrected. I wonder what action the department of corporate and consumer affairs will take.

I repeat, we do not mind other people stealing our clothes, but we object to the way in which they sometimes wear them. For example, we question very much the tops of pyjamas being worn when the bottom of the garment is not worn at the same time. As we look at the proposal before us we are bound to think it is a weak type of legislation we are being asked to consider. But having played a large part in getting this vehicle on the highway, underpowered as it may be, we shall do our best as a group to see that it goes in the right direction in the interests, we trust, of the Canadian consumer. I wish the minister well in his endeavours and I am hopeful that he will at least bring energy to his new task.
I should like to devote the rest of my remarks to a subject which I hope he and the department will take up rapidly, namely the protection of a large number of Canadian consumers from the effects of advertising. In particular, I wish to refer to a matter connected with consumer advertising which has prompted me to introduce three separate bills into this house, each one being, I would hope, a protective measure for Canadian consumers of tobacco products, specifically cigarettes.
It is a known fact that cigarette companies are spending millions of dollars every year to induce young Canadians to begin smoking, this at a time when every health department in the world is agreed that there is a link between cigarette smoking and cancer, heart troubles and related afflictions. I think a good step to further protection of the consumers would be for the new department to take up this question and see to it that until the cigarette industry can produce a safe cigarette its advertising be examined and, if necessary, regulated by the appropriate department of government.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I wish to quote briefly from a statement made by Norman Delarue, assistant professor in surgery at the University of Toronto, published in Health which is the organ of The Health League of Canada. He says:
The death rates from heavy smokers are 30 to 50 times those in non-smokers and, as a recent 27053-197
Corporate and Consumer Affairs
Canadian study of the risk demonstrated, the overall death rate from lung cancer is 1,400 per cent (15 times) higher in smokers than in nonsmokers ...
However, despite the tremendously increased frequency with which lung cancer may develop, the cigarette smoker is at still greater risk from chronic bronchitis and emphysema, both of which show an identical statistical relationship with the cigarette smoking habit.
If I may, Mr. Chairman, I would like to give another brief quotation on this subject, from the New York Times of Monday, August 21, last. This refers to a United States government report strengthening and extending the findings of its 1964 report on smoking and disease, and one paragraph of which reads:
Further, the report states, the new evidence indicates that cigarette smoking is responsible for 11 million cases of chronic illness in the country, 77 million days lost from work and 306 million days of restricted activity each year.
We can get the approximate Canadian figures by taking 10 per cent of the American figures.
In brief, I think that one of the great consumer protection fields which needs attention is that in which millions of Canadians are smoking a product which is unsafe, which advertising induces them to do, advertising which is permitted and indeed carried by a public agency of the government, the C.B.C. I urge that action be taken by the new department of consumer affairs in that area. As I said earlier, I wish the minister and his supporters well in getting this new and overdue organization on the road, and we will do our best to keep it going in the right direction.

Corporate and Consumer Affairs able to please everybody. Having sat here this morning and this afternoon, and having been given new responsibilities in a department which will be called the department of corporate and consumer affairs I now know it will be difficult to please anybody.
On the one hand I listened to the official opposition, with its talented array of speakers. In a philosophical way they advanced the argument that there really was no need for such a department, that it was clearly more government expense, more bureaucracy, intervention in the marketplace where this was not required because, after all, business has as its prime motive looking after consumers, because business sells to consumers. In other words they said this was a rather useless exercise but they would go along with it because there might be some useful corrolar-ies or accessories to it if only by way of co-ordination.
On the other hand I listened to the N.D.P. who felt that the resolution and the suggestion of legislation did not go nearly far enough, even to the extent that the hon. member for New Westminster had me running around without my pants by the time he finished his speech this afternoon. speechtext:
The N.D.P. seems to want a department that will intervene at any time, anywhere, for almost any reason, in any domain of the economy or any phase of our national life. The hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands suggested that I ought to take up the cudgels against pollution. This of course happens to be the responsibility of a department of government, and further the responsibility is shared between federal and provincial jurisdictions. The hon. member also wanted me to take up the cudgels against automobile manufacturers. That properly falls within another portfolio, and again there is divided jurisdiction with respect to highways and automobile safety.
The whole constitutional problem never seems to enter the minds of the N.D.P., and the fact remains that any department of corporate and consumer affairs will be facing certain limitations because of divided jurisdiction. In fact probably the greater share of the responsibility for the consumer in this country lies at the provincial level, particularly with respect to the retail and distributing end of the marketplace.

Then, of course, in the eyes of the N.D.P. I found myself solely responsible for the cost of living. In so far as the federal government is responsible, I suppose that is a joint and several responsibility. I think there is no doubt that the cost of living is the major concern of the Canadian people at the present time, and despite the remarks of the hon. member for Yukon and of the hon. member for Bow River we in the government have read with great seriousness the fourth annual report of the Economic Council of Canada.
I may say that we have sliced millions of dollars off our contemplated spending, and I think Canadian taxpayers should be well aware that only one third of the total tax dollar is spent by the federal government at this time and that over two thirds-and that proportion has been rising in recent years-is now being spent by provincial and municipal governments.
I think an economist of the stature of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands is aware that the cost of living and price rises are due to other factors than government, that they depend on international economic developments, on international trade, the laws of supply and demand in the country, the shortage or the availability of capital, the extend and rapidity of growth in the country, our efforts to maintain full employment, and so on. So, flattered as I am to be singled out for attention, I want to assure him that the new department cannot in reasonable circumstances be held solely to account for these.
We again heard talk about a prices review board, but no talk about a corollary which would have to be added to that, a costs or wages review board, and no suggestion how any enforcement would be made, or where the constitutional validity for that would be, even if we were to accept the rather hesitant suggestion from the hon. member for Peace River that economic crisis might constitute a sufficient emergency within the decision of the courts so as to bring the control of prices in such a time within federal jurisdiction.
On the one hand we had the philosophical approach that suggests we do not need any government representation for the consumer at the federal level, and the other approach that the new department should virtually be a big brother to the consumers, all 20 million Canadians, in almost every aspect of national, provincial and municipal life. I want to say in answer to the opposition-

If I could clear up this point first, I would be glad to do so later. I should like to say to the hon. member, particularly, that the measure which is contemplated by the resolution is not providing for a new department in the strict sense. The present Department of the Registrar General and the agencies now grouped within it will be continued under a department with a new name, the department of corporate and consumer affairs, to which will be added two further responsibilities; first, the responsibility to coordinate programs for consumer affairs at the federal level, initiate new programs, and so on; second, the responsibility for representing the federal government in the area of corporate securities. That fulfils quite properly the recommendation of the Economic Council of Canada in its interim report on consumer affairs.
If the hon. member for the Yukon would look at page 25 of this report he would find the recommendation that legislation be created to provide for an administrative unit in the Department of the Registrar General whose chief concern will be the efficient administration of these provisions, namely the pi'ovisions relating to consumer affairs. This legislation provides for that administrative unit in the Department of the Registrar General who, hereafter, will be the minister of corporate and consumer affairs. The recommendation is being followed to the letter.
I should like to say to the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Bow River in particular, in answer to some of their suggestions, that this department will not be a bureaucratic monster. On one occasion I said that if you want to use the vocabulary of the octopus of government, this is not a new tentacle; it is a rearrangement of the existing tentacles, and no more. It will provide for co-operation between all existing agencies of the government which are now found in other departments. It is not a centralization at this stage.
The hon. member for Yukon is right in pointing out that the Economic Council of Canada suggested that we look very carefully at the matter of which agencies should be grouped together. We have made no prejudgment concerning whether the food and drug directorate, whether the weights and measures branch of the Department of Trade and 27053-1971

I am very grateful to the committee. I will attempt to summarize my remarks as quickly as I can. In other words, we will be responsible for co-ordination and initiation. Administrative centralization will be left to future judgment. This is the reason we will await the judgment of the interdepartmental committee of which my parliamentary secretary spoke, which is now in operation grouping together those departments which have an interest in consumer affairs. When we have the advice of that interdepartmental committee we will be able to determine which agencies might be best administered by the new department.
I should like to say also that this department will not involve more government spending. When I spoke on my estimates I said that this year the department would have an expenditure of $8 million, less $6 million by way of revenue in respect of patent applications, bankruptcies, incorporation applications, and so on; so, the cost to the Canadian taxpayer will be between $1.5 million and $2 million. There will be no additional cost of any significance because, as I said, aside from the hiring of certain specialists in the area of consumer affairs most of the staff is available in the various agencies of the federal government.
I should like to say to the members of the New Democratic party that as best I can within the constitutional responsibilities given to me, and with the responsibilities given to me under the legislation which will be deposited and tabled in this house, I intend to represent the demand side of the market, and equalize the market forces between consumer and investor, on the one hand, and the supply side on the other, in order to give better bargaining strength to the demand side of the market. They suggested I am not prepared to
October 13, 1967

Corporate and Consumer Affairs intervene as much as I should. They recited some areas where I thought intervention would be justified and where I would be prepared, and would have the power, to intervene. These included collusion in pricing, monopolistic prices, areas where there might be deception or fraud, areas where public health or safety is concerned and areas where more education or research is needed to equalize the relationship between supply and demand. I am prepared to do that. At no time during the afternoon did they suggest where that statement was wrong or where it should be supplemented. I look forward on second reading to hearing their suggestions in that regard.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say that on second reading I will be glad to take the house through the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada as they affect the department of corporate and consumer affairs. I think I will be able to establish to the satisfaction of the house, when it sits as a house, that each one of the recommendations on page 19 and following has been considered and is reflected in the bill, and how it is reflected. In certain areas we have not accepted the whole breadth of the recommendations, but in many more areas we have gone beyond the recommendations. An interdepartmental committee has been set up. The department will represent the consumers' point of view; there will be sections for information and research. There will be that co-ordination, I hope, for which the Economic Council called, and so on, through the report.
The members of the house certainly will receive from me the information to which they are entitled, not only concerning the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada, but also concerning the recommendations of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons of which my learned friend from Vancouver-Burrard was the cochairman. Finally, I should like to say to the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke that he need not be disturbed about my not being able to get together with my seatmate for the moment, the Minister of Agriculture. This department will not have as its purpose the displacement of any other interests. The other economic interests in this country already are represented by government departments. The farmers are represented by the Department of Agriculture; the fishermen are represented by the Department of Fisheries; the businessmen are represented by the Department of Industry and the Department of Trade and Commerce, and so on.

speechtext: Who represents the taxpayer?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF DEPARTMENT, APPOINTMENT OF PERSONNEL, ETC.
speechtext:
As I say, this is the only department which represents the demand side of the market, particularly in having as its pertinent reference the investor and consumer. There is no question that the other interests which already are represented will in any way be displaced. In establishing a department which will have among its responsibilities that of consumer affairs, we will not be displacing other interests; we will be adding a new dimension in government to meet what we think is a public demand for new services, new information and fresh guidance. I feel that each Canadian in his capacity as a consumer is now moving forward, insisting, and demanding that his or her interest be represented by government, just as the workman, the businessman and the farmer are already represented here.
Protection of the consumer is not new in the federal government. He or she is represented already in several agencies, but the new complexities and great proliferation of products in so many areas, and in new areas, demands a new look at the policies which are necessary to protect the consumer. My parliamentary secretary recited some of the basic rights which we will recognize and which President Kennedy in his first message to Congress in 1962 related to the consumers' interest. I might say that what we are trying to achieve here by increasing ministerial authority on the one hand or ministerial responsibility on the other goes far beyond what has been accomplished in the United States. He spoke of the right of safety, the right to be informed, the right to choose and the right to be heard. I hope that this department will be responsible to the consumer, will represent the consumer and give the consumer a new voice at the ministerial level of the federal government.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-10, to amend the Canada Corporations Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to the house for suspending private members hour and for allowing me to introduce this bill once again. The bill constitutes amendments to the 1934 statute, the Canada Corporations Act, which received its first major amendments in 1965. In 1965 it was necessary to bring in a few so-called housekeeping amendments. We have since found after a little more than a year of operation that the act requires a few more housekeeping amendments. There is nothing of significance or policy in this bill.
The bill has 10 clauses. Clauses 1, 2 and 9 are long overdue and have no connection at all with the 1965 amendments. Clauses 3 and 7 are required to clear away difficulties unforeseen in 1965 but which are posing major problems to the public and the department. Clauses 6 and 8 are the most important ones. They deeply affect the interpretation of the amendments made in 1965 to section 121B and 128A which were drafted separately. There was little opportunity to make the necessary and consequential amendments in order to correspond with the general interpretation section of the act.
Clauses 4, 5 and 10 are merely corrections of clerical errors or oversights that have been found over the years. After we get into committee I will be able to explain the reason for each amendment as we consider the individual clauses.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would refer the minister to section 125 of the act. I appreciate the good intentions of the minister, but the law is there now; it does not need any tightening up. Section 125 (4) of the act provides as follows:
Where a company makes default in complying with any requirement of this section, it is liable to a fine not exceeding twenty dollars for every day during which the default continues, and every director and officer of the company who knowingly and wilfully authorizes or permits the default is liable to the like penalty, and such fines may be recoverable on summary conviction.
I believe that the stipulations set forth in section 125 of the act are there so that the public can be informed of at least the fundamental structure of the company. This is a document that is publicly displayed so that those dealing with corporations incorporated under the act will at least know the names of the directors, the manner in which the company is incorporated, whether it is a company in good standing, and like information. In my

submission, Mr. Chairman, there need be no tightening up of the law, because the law is there now. All that is required is that it should be followed up by one of the officials in the department whose responsibility it is, and must have been for several years, to do so.
It is surely a simple matter to diary-date the due dates of these returns and red flag those that do not send in the annual returns on the due date. If they are not submitted, the company should be written to and told [DOT]-as a matter of courtesy they are entitled to a warning-that if the return is not completed within a week, proceedings will be commenced against them. I know, and the minister knows, that for years some corporations have been negligent in this respect. This is one of the reasons I am delighted to see that the amendment stipulates a period of two years. But they can still go back two years without having this section come into operation. However, subsection (4) of section 125 provides for a penalty to be imposed in the case of companies that fail to file a return on the due date.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SHARE ISSUES, BY-LAWS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member probably already knows this, but I have been advised by my officials that of these defaulters by far the greater majority of the companies are no longer operating. They become mere shells. Of course, if they were operating they would have to file returns in order to stay in business. But they are not operating. The directors are spread all over the place. The advice I have been given-and I am looking into this matter-is that it would cost the Canadian taxpayers far more to prosecute people all across the country connected with dead corporate shells, which are no longer dealing with the public or anybody else, than the revenues obtained from such prosecutions.
I have asked that the entire enforcement sections of the act that are linked with the disclosure areas be rationalized, if I may use that term. I can assure the hon. member that in by far the greater majority of these cases the public would have little interest in disclosure, since the companies have gone out of business. They have failed to surrender their charters. If they have charters they would of course have to bring themselves up to date.
